newsitem.title: USA: China grain self sufficiency drive seen temporary.
newsitem.headline: China grain self sufficiency drive seen temporary.

text.p: China's grain imports will be lower this marketing year due to a recent decision by the Chinese government to move to greater self sufficiency but the trend will probably be short-lived, said the Agriculture Department's senior China analyst.

"There's going to be a gap between what they can produce and what the demand is ... the question is how big the gap will be," said Fred Crook, China specialist for USDA's Economic Research Service, in an interview with Reuters.
Crook recently returned from a two week trip to China where he met with government and grain trade officials and toured parts of China's key northeastern corn growing region.

Crook, who has been an observer and analyst of Chinese agricultural policy for over 30 years, said the government this year has shifted back to a self-sufficiency policy after adopting a more market oriented stance the last few years.

He said abundant grain harvests this year in China, surplus domestic grain stocks and high world crop prices this past year have encouraged the government to adopt the more inwards looking policy and have discouraged continued large imports, at least for the time being.

Crook estimated that China currently has about six months worth of grain in storage, and said the big question is if China will continue to import moderate quantities and build up stocks, or tighten imports even more and draw down on its supplies.

Chinese corn imports could drop to zero this year from over four million tonnes just two years ago, said Crook. He said that China may export corn in the coming months, although the timing of that is very uncertain.
But the analyst said that in the long run, the shift to self sufficiency is a "step backwards" and will not succeed.

"This policy is costly ... they can do it, but at a high cost, and only for a period of time," said Crook. "My guess is that in two to three years, they will probably return to a more normal marketing pattern -- this is an unusual period."

Crook said that China has advantages in the more labor intensive production of fruits and vegetables, but that the United States, Australia, Argentina, Canada and the European Union can all grow grains and soybeans cheaper.

He said China would be smart to concentrate on the production and export of its lucrative fresh produce to gain revenue to import grains. "China can make a lot of money from vegetable exports to buy grain," said Crook.

The analyst said demand for better diets in China is still growing, especially in the bustling urban areas. He said the poultry sector is currently growing faster than the red meat sector, and feels this will continue for some time.

Crook said agricultural growth in China will depend largely on how much is invested in the agricultural sector, and that right now the Chinese government does not appear to have agriculture at the high end of its investment priorities.
"Agriculture is a poor cousin," said Crook. "It's at the end of the line ... It just doesn't get the resources."
